Topics covered: Handling time series in R: ts objects, dates and aggregation, subsetting, lags and differences, combining series, missing values, time plots and decomposition, and the tidy toolkit (tsibble, feasts, timetk).
Data: sales_data.csv, daily sales for several stores (columns date, store_id, sales), stored in the repository’s data/ folder. Packages: tidyverse, tsibble, feasts, timetk, knitr, here.
Code
library(tidyverse)   # dplyr, ggplot2, readr, lubridate
library(tsibble)     # tidy time series class: index + key
library(feasts)      # features and statistics for tsibbles
library(timetk)      # tidy plotting and diagnostics for tibbles
library(knitr)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))

data_file <- here::here("data", "sales_data.csv")

title: TS Intro
text:
Overview of the key concepts
A time series is a set of observations indexed by time, where the order matters and neighbouring values are usually related. Before any modelling, the data have to be stored in a form that R recognises as a time series, so that it knows the spacing of the observations and where each one falls in the seasonal cycle.
The ts class. A ts object is a numeric vector with three extra attributes: start, end and frequency. The frequency is the number of observations per cycle (12 for monthly data with a yearly cycle, 4 for quarterly, 52 for weekly). start = c(2021, 1) means period 1 of 2021, so for monthly data January 2021. Periods are numbered from 1, and the second element of start can never exceed the frequency. Once these attributes are set, functions such as window(), lag(), diff(), cycle() and decompose() all know how the data are spaced.
Aggregation. Data are often collected at a finer resolution than we want to model. Daily sales can be summed to monthly totals or averaged to weekly means. The choice of resolution decides which patterns are visible: daily data show a weekly cycle and a yearly cycle, while monthly totals hide the weekly cycle completely.
Lags and differences. The lag operator shifts a series in time, \(BY_t = Y_{t-1}\). Differencing removes structure: the first difference \(\nabla Y_t = Y_t - Y_{t-1}\) removes a linear trend, and the seasonal difference \(\nabla_{12} Y_t = Y_t - Y_{t-12}\) removes a stable 12-month pattern. These are the building blocks of ARIMA and SARIMA models later in the section.
Decomposition. An additive decomposition writes the series as
\[
Y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t,
\]
a trend-cycle \(T_t\), a seasonal component \(S_t\) that repeats every \(m\) periods and sums to zero over a cycle, and a remainder \(R_t\). Classical decomposition estimates the trend with a centred moving average, then averages the detrended values for each season. STL does the same job with local regression (loess), lets the seasonal pattern change slowly over time, and is more robust to outliers.
The tidy toolkit. A tsibble is a data frame with an explicit index (the time variable) and key (which series each row belongs to), so many series can live in one table. It also distinguishes implicit gaps (missing rows) from explicit missing values (rows containing NA). feasts provides seasonal plots, ACFs, STL and feature extraction on tsibbles, and timetk produces similar diagnostics directly from an ordinary tibble.

Question 7: What is wrong with each call?
Q1. ts(x, start = c(2023, 13), frequency = 12) Monthly data have only 12 periods per year, so the second element of start cannot exceed 12. “Period 13 of 2023” does not exist; it should roll over to January 2024. Fix: ts(x, start = c(2024, 1), frequency = 12).
Q2. ts(x, start = 2023, frequency = 12) For sub-annual data (frequency > 1), start should give both the year and the period within the year. A single number is ambiguous. Fix: ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12).
Q3. ts(x, start = c(2023, 0), frequency = 12) Periods are numbered from 1, so period 0 does not exist; January is period 1. Fix: ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12).
Q4. ts(x, start = c(2023, 2), frequency = 4) “Period 2” depends on the frequency: with frequency = 4 it means Q2, not February. If the data are monthly, the frequency must match their real spacing. Fix: ts(x, start = c(2023, 2), frequency = 12).
Q5. ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12.5) The frequency counts observations per cycle, so it should be a whole number. Most methods built on ts objects (seasonal differencing, decompose(), seasonal ARIMA) need an integer frequency. Fix: ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12).
Q6. ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12, deltat = 1/12) frequency and deltat describe the same thing from two directions (deltat = 1/frequency), so giving both is redundant. Fix: give only one, e.g. ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12).
Q7. ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 365) frequency = 365 declares daily data. If x holds monthly values, every value is placed at the wrong point in the yearly cycle. Fix: ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12).
Q8. window(x, start = c(2023, 13)) window() can only extract periods that exist inside the series’ range, and month 13 does not exist. Fix: start at a valid point inside the series, e.g. window(x, start = c(2024, 1)).
Q9. decompose(ts(x, frequency = 1)) With frequency = 1 there is no seasonal cycle, so there is no seasonal component to estimate. decompose() also needs at least two complete cycles. Fix: use the series’ real seasonal frequency, e.g. decompose(ts(x, frequency = 12)).

title: TS Intro
text:
Implementation in R
To understand what decompose() is doing, I wrote the classical additive decomposition from first principles and checked it against the built-in function on the monthly S001 series.

Trend. With an even period \(m = 12\), a plain 12-term moving average is not centred on a month. A \(2 \times 12\) moving average fixes this: it is a 13-term weighted average with weights \(\tfrac{1}{24}\) on the two end months and \(\tfrac{1}{12}\) on the 11 in between, \[
\hat T_t = \frac{1}{12}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}Y_{t-6} + Y_{t-5} + \dots + Y_{t+5} + \tfrac{1}{2}Y_{t+6}\right).
\] The first and last six months have no trend estimate.
Seasonal component. Detrend, \(Y_t - \hat T_t\), average the detrended values for each calendar month, then centre the 12 averages so they sum to zero.
Remainder. \(\hat R_t = Y_t - \hat T_t - \hat S_t\).



Code
my_decompose <- function(y) {
  m <- frequency(y)
  w <- if (m %% 2 == 0) c(0.5, rep(1, m - 1), 0.5) / m else rep(1, m) / m
  trend <- stats::filter(y, w, sides = 2)

  detrended <- y - trend
  s_means <- tapply(detrended, cycle(y), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  s_means <- s_means - mean(s_means)            # seasonal effects sum to zero
  seasonal <- ts(s_means[cycle(y)], start = start(y), frequency = m)

  list(trend = trend, seasonal = seasonal, random = y - trend - seasonal,
       figure = s_means)
}

mine  <- my_decompose(sales_ts)
built <- decompose(sales_ts)

max_diff <- c(
  Trend     = max(abs(mine$trend    - built$trend),    na.rm = TRUE),
  Seasonal  = max(abs(mine$seasonal - built$seasonal), na.rm = TRUE),
  Remainder = max(abs(mine$random   - built$random),   na.rm = TRUE)
)

title: TS Intro
text:
Reflection
What was most challenging: Keeping track of the different ways R represents time. A ts object stores time as decimal years with a frequency attribute, a Date column stores calendar dates, and a tsibble uses an index and key. Each has its own rules: start periods are numbered from 1, frequency must match the real spacing of the data, and daily data need the seasonal period stated explicitly because there is more than one cycle. The lag() clash was the most confusing. stats::lag() shifts the time attribute while dplyr::lag() shifts the values, and which one runs depends on which packages are loaded.
What I now understand: Getting the structure of a time series right is part of the analysis, not a preliminary step. The frequency decides what cycle(), seasonal differencing and decomposition do, so a wrong frequency produces output that looks plausible but is meaningless (as in Question 7). Aggregation is a modelling choice too: summing to monthly removes the weekly cycle entirely. The difference between implicit gaps and explicit NAs in a tsibble explained why filling gaps has to happen before aggregating.
Advantages and limitations of the methods:

Advantages: Base ts objects are simple and are what most classical functions (arima, decompose, HoltWinters) expect. The tidy tools handle many series at once through the key, deal with irregular dates and gaps explicitly, and make seasonal plots for multiple periods easy.
Limitations: A ts object supports only one regular frequency, so it cannot represent daily data with both weekly and yearly cycles. Classical decomposition assumes a fixed seasonal pattern and loses the trend at the ends of the series. Filling missing days with a store mean is convenient for exploration but would bias any model fitted afterwards.

Links: Project 1 (ARIMA and SARIMA on tourism nights sold) builds on these tools, starting from a monthly ts object, a time plot, a seasonal subseries plot and an STL decomposition before differencing. See also the Week 1 journal entry.

text:
NoteExecutive summary



Title: Modelling the COVID-19 shock in South African accommodation demand
Section and topic: Section 2. Exponential smoothing (ETS), regression with ARIMA errors and intervention (transfer function) terms, state-space models and the Kalman filter.
Type of project: Model comparison on real-world data, with a profile likelihood search for the intervention decay rate. It extends Project 1 on the same series and the same test set, so the results of the two projects can be compared directly.
Question: In Project 1 the COVID-19 months were either kept, which broke the SARIMA model, or deleted, which threw information away. Can the shock be modelled instead, and does that, or adding the exchange rate as a predictor, give better forecasts of accommodation demand than ETS and the Project 1 SARIMA?
Data: Real-world, publicly available data. Statistics South Africa, Tourist Accommodation release P6410, series B64100 (stay unit nights sold, total industry), and the monthly average rand per US dollar exchange rate (FRED series EXSFUS), January 2015 to June 2026. Full source details are in Section 2.1.
Methods: ETS; regression with ARIMA errors containing deterministic seasonal dummies and COVID intervention terms (a geometrically decaying shock, two pulses and a level shift), with the decay rate chosen by profile likelihood; the same model with the log exchange rate added, forecast both ex ante and ex post; a basic structural model (local level, slope and seasonal) fitted by maximum likelihood with the Kalman filter, with the COVID months treated as missing. All models go through the Box and Jenkins loop and are compared with the Project 1 SARIMA and the seasonal naive benchmark on the July 2024 to June 2026 test set.
Key findings: See Section 8.1.
What I would do differently: Use rolling-origin cross-validation for the final comparison, and estimate the decay rate jointly with the other parameters rather than on a grid.
Detailed analysis: the sections below.

title: Project 3: Modelling the COVID-19 Shock in South African Accommodation Demand
text:
4.1 Why deterministic seasonality
In Project 1, every seasonal ARIMA model fitted with the COVID months included estimated a seasonal MA coefficient at or near -1. A seasonal MA factor \((1 - L^{12})\) that cancels the seasonal difference \((1 - L^{12})\) is the classic sign that the seasonal pattern is fixed rather than evolving, so that seasonal differencing is over-differencing. The seasonal plots in Project 1 point the same way. In this model the seasonality is therefore represented by 11 monthly dummy variables, while a first difference in the errors handles the wandering level.

title: Project 3: Modelling the COVID-19 Shock in South African Accommodation Demand
text:
4.2 Modelling the shock
The intervention terms follow the transfer function idea from Chapter 2: the effect of an event is described by a small set of explanatory variables whose shape reflects how the event unfolded. With \(t_0\) = April 2020 and everything on the log scale:

Decaying shock: \(D_t(\delta) = \delta^{\,t - t_0}\) for \(t \ge t_0\) and 0 before. Its coefficient \(\omega\) is the immediate effect in April 2020, which then dies out geometrically at rate \(\delta\). This is the transfer function \(\omega / (1 - \delta L)\) applied to a pulse at \(t_0\).
Pulses for March 2020 (lockdown started on 27 March, so the month was only partly affected) and May 2020 (the industry stayed almost completely closed, so the bottom of the collapse lasted two months rather than one).
Level shift: \(S_t = 1\) for \(t \ge t_0\), allowing a permanent difference between the pre-COVID and post-COVID levels.

The model is
\[
\log y_t = \sum_{j=1}^{11} \gamma_j M_{jt} + \omega D_t(\delta) + \kappa_1 P^{\text{Mar20}}_t + \kappa_2 P^{\text{May20}}_t + \lambda S_t + \eta_t, \qquad (1 - L)\,\phi(L)\,\eta_t = \theta(L)\,\varepsilon_t ,
\]
where \(M_{jt}\) are monthly dummies and \(\eta_t\) follows an ARIMA(\(p\), 1, \(q\)) process.


Code
covid_vars <- function(df, delta) {
  k0 <- month_num(shock_month)
  df |>
    mutate(k     = month_num(Month) - k0,
           decay = if_else(k >= 0, delta^pmax(k, 0), 0),
           mar20 = as.numeric(k == -1),
           may20 = as.numeric(k == 1),
           step  = as.numeric(k >= 0))
}

section: 4.3 Choosing the decay rate by profile likelihood
text:
4.3 Choosing the decay rate by profile likelihood
The decay rate \(\delta\) enters the model non-linearly, so it cannot be estimated by ARIMA() directly. Instead I profile it: for each \(\delta\) on a grid from 0.70 to 0.96, the model is fitted (with the ARIMA error orders chosen by AICc) and the AICc recorded. The value of \(\delta\) with the smallest AICc is used. Because \(\delta\) is estimated, the model really has one more parameter than ARIMA() reports; this does not change the ranking along the grid.


Code
delta_grid <- seq(0.70, 0.96, by = 0.02)

profile <- bind_rows(lapply(delta_grid, function(dl) {
  f <- covid_vars(train, dl) |>
    model(reg = ARIMA(log(nights) ~ season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step +
                        pdq(d = 1) + PDQ(0, 0, 0)))
  tibble(delta = dl,
         AICc  = glance(f)$AICc,
         spec  = fabletools::model_sum(f$reg[[1]]$fit))
}))

delta_hat <- profile$delta[which.min(profile$AICc)]




Code
ggplot(profile, aes(delta, AICc)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = filter(profile, delta == delta_hat), colour = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  labs(x = expression(delta), y = "AICc")








Figure 2: Profile of AICc against the decay rate. The selected value is marked in red.





The AICc is minimised at \(\hat\delta\) = 0.76 (Figure 2). A decay rate of 0.76 means that the temporary part of the shock halves every 2.5 months and has fallen to 4% of its initial size after a year.

text:
4.6 Does the exchange rate help?
Because the model is in logs, the coefficient on log USD/ZAR is an elasticity: a 10% weakening of the rand is associated with a change of about 2.7% in nights sold, holding the seasonal and COVID terms fixed. The estimate is 0.270 (p 0.175), and the AICc gets worse from -227.1 to -225.9. The exchange rate does not add significant information once the seasonal pattern and the COVID shock are accounted for, which is not surprising since most stays are domestic and the effect of the rand on foreign arrivals works with a lag. The model is in first differences, so the coefficient measures the effect of changes in the rand on changes in demand within the same month.
A model with an explanatory variable has a practical catch: to forecast nights sold, I need future values of the exchange rate, which are not known when the forecast is made. Two versions are therefore evaluated:

Ex ante (realistic): the exchange rate is assumed to stay at its last observed value (June 2024), a naive forecast.
Ex post (optimistic): the actual exchange rate during the test period is used. This is not a genuine forecast, since it uses information that would not have been available in June 2024. It shows the best the model could do if the rand were forecast perfectly.

title: Project 3: Modelling the COVID-19 Shock in South African Accommodation Demand
text:
6.2 Results
Overall ranking. The lowest test RMSE is achieved by the Reg model (98.8 thousand nights). Among the models that passed the diagnostic step, the best is the Reg model. For reference, the Project 1 SARIMA has an RMSE of 101.6 and the seasonal naive benchmark 132.6.
ETS. ETS reaches an RMSE of 130.0, beating the seasonal naive benchmark even though it was fitted to data that include the COVID collapse. Its fast-moving level lets it recover from the shock without any special treatment, which a SARIMA with the COVID months included could not do in Project 1. Its 95% intervals are, however, wider than those of the regression model, because the COVID months still inflate its estimated error variance (mean width 2,292 against 1,060 thousand nights).
Regression with intervention terms. Modelling the shock explicitly gives an RMSE of 98.8 and a MAPE of 4.51%, better than the Project 1 SARIMA that simply deleted the COVID months. Its intervals cover 100% of the test months at the 95% level and 100% at the 80% level. The two approaches reach very similar forecast accuracy, which makes sense: by June 2024 the temporary part of the shock had almost disappeared (\(\hat\delta^{\,50} \approx\) 1.1e-06), so the main forecasting information in both models comes from the post-COVID level and the seasonal pattern. The advantage of the regression model is not mainly accuracy but interpretation: it estimates the size, shape and persistence of the shock (Figure 4) instead of discarding it.
Exchange rate. Adding the rand changes the RMSE to 106.2 ex ante and 130.3 ex post. Neither version improves on the model without the exchange rate. The gap between the ex ante and ex post results is a reminder that a regression model’s forecasts are only as good as the forecasts of its explanatory variables.
State-space models. The full BSM has an RMSE of 184.7 and the fixed slope version 102.9. The difference comes from the slope: in the full model the slope adapts to the steep recovery in 2022 and 2023 and this growth is extrapolated forward, whereas with a fixed slope the long-run average growth is used. This shows that two models with almost identical likelihoods can give very different forecasts, because the likelihood is dominated by one-step-ahead fit while forecasts two years ahead depend on how the trend is extrapolated. Both BSMs failed the residual diagnostics, so even if their forecasts happen to be competitive on this test set, they are not candidates under the Box and Jenkins rule.

title: Project 3: Modelling the COVID-19 Shock in South African Accommodation Demand
text:
8.1 Key findings

Deterministic seasonality. The seasonal MA coefficient of -1 found in Project 1 is evidence of a fixed seasonal pattern. Replacing seasonal differencing with monthly dummies gave a regression model with white noise residuals (Ljung and Box p = 0.556).
The shock can be modelled parsimoniously. A decaying intervention with \(\hat\delta\) = 0.76 (half-life about 2.5 months), two pulses and a level shift capture the collapse and recovery with five parameters instead of 25 deleted months.
Forecast accuracy. The best model on the test set was Reg, and the best model that also passed the diagnostics was Reg. The regression model (RMSE 98.8) and the Project 1 SARIMA (RMSE 101.6) were close, because by 2024 the temporary part of the shock had died out.
ETS is a robust baseline. Without any special treatment of COVID, ETS reached an RMSE of 130.0, because its level adapts quickly.
The exchange rate had an estimated elasticity of 0.270 (p 0.175). Ex ante, it did not improve the forecasts.
The BSM interpolates the level through the COVID gap and its forecasts depend strongly on whether the slope is allowed to vary, but its innovations were not white noise, so it failed the Box and Jenkins diagnostic step.

title: Project 3: Modelling the COVID-19 Shock in South African Accommodation Demand
text:
8.2 Issues and limitations

Single test period. All comparisons rest on one 24 month test set. Project 1 showed that rolling-origin cross-validation gives a more reliable ranking; with more time I would repeat it here, although refitting the BSM and repeating the \(\delta\) profile at every origin is slow.
Choice of intervention shape. The decay, pulses and step were chosen by looking at the data, so there is a risk of over-fitting the shape of the shock to this particular series. The AICc profile guards against some of this, but the pulse months were picked by eye.
Confounding with the exchange rate. The rand depreciated sharply in March and April 2020, at the same time as the lockdown. Adding the exchange rate after the intervention terms avoids attributing the COVID collapse to the rand, but it also means the exchange rate effect is estimated mainly from the non-COVID months.
Same-month effect only. The exchange rate enters without a lag. Foreign visitors book weeks or months ahead, so a lagged effect would be more realistic and would also make ex ante forecasting easier for short horizons.
BSM limitations in StructTS(). The irregular variance was estimated at zero and the innovations were autocorrelated. A more flexible state-space model (for example in dlm or KFAS, with an AR(1) component or explanatory variables in the state equation) would be the natural next step.
Profile likelihood standard errors. Treating \(\hat\delta\) as known when computing the other standard errors understates their uncertainty.

title: Project 3: Modelling the COVID-19 Shock in South African Accommodation Demand
text:
8.3 What I would do differently
I would estimate \(\delta\) jointly with the other parameters by maximising the likelihood directly, use rolling-origin cross-validation for the final ranking, try a lagged exchange rate, and build the state-space model in dlm so that an AR(1) component and the intervention terms could be added to it, combining the strengths of the regression and state-space approaches in one model.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
NoteExecutive summary



Title: Forecasting South African accommodation demand with ARIMA and SARIMA models
Section and topic: Section 1. Benchmarks, stationarity and differencing, ARMA, ARIMA and SARIMA models, the Box and Jenkins workflow, forecast evaluation.
Type of project: Implementation and model comparison on real-world data.
Question: How much forecast accuracy is gained by moving from simple benchmark methods to ARMA, ARIMA and seasonal ARIMA models for monthly stay unit nights sold in South Africa, and how sensitive is that gain to the way the COVID-19 structural break is handled?
Data: Real-world, publicly available data from Statistics South Africa (Stats SA), Tourist Accommodation statistical release P6410, series B64100 (stay unit nights sold, total industry, thousands), monthly. Analysis window January 2015 to June 2026. Full source details are in Section 2.1.
Methods: The analysis follows the ARIMA modelling procedure from the lectures (plot, transform, difference, identify, estimate, check residuals, forecast). The COVID months (March 2020 to March 2022) are treated as missing, so all models are estimated from the pre- and post-COVID data only; fitting the same models with the COVID months kept is reported as a sensitivity check. The transformation and the orders of differencing are chosen from the non-COVID data using time plots, the Guerrero estimate of the Box–Cox parameter, ACF/PACF plots and unit root tests. Candidate SARIMA models are identified by hand from the ACF and PACF, refined by an AIC search over neighbouring orders, and compared with the model chosen automatically by ARIMA(). Each candidate is checked with residual plots, Ljung–Box tests and its AR and MA roots. The candidates are then compared with four benchmarks (mean, naive, seasonal naive, drift) and simpler ARMA and ARIMA models on a 24-month test set (RMSE, MAE, MAPE, MASE, interval coverage) and by expanding-window rolling-origin cross-validation over horizons of 1 to 12 months.
Target variable: This analysis focuses on stay unit nights sold. This was chosen over income level and occupancy rate because it appears to be the most consistent. Occupancy rate can change when room supply changes anc income can be disrupted by inflation or other general increases. Unit nights sold tells a very clear demand picture with minimal factors affecting the quality of the variable over the years.
Key findings: See Section 9.1. In short: with the COVID months left in the data, the seasonal ARIMA models are no better than the seasonal naive benchmark, because the collapse in April 2020 dominates the estimated variance and distorts the parameters. Treating the COVID window as missing gives a stable SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 “airline” model with well behaved residuals, and that model gives the most accurate forecasts on both the test set and in cross-validation.
What I would do differently: Model the shock explicitly with intervention variables (planned for Project 3), and compare the expanding window with a sliding window that forgets the pre-COVID years.
Detailed analysis: the sections below.

text:
4.1 The Box and Jenkins workflow
The modelling follows the Box and Jenkins workflow from the notes. Each step maps to a part of this report:

Plot the data: the time plot, seasonal plots and STL decomposition in the exploratory analysis.
Difference until approximately stationary: one seasonal and one first difference of log nights sold, chosen from the unit root tests and the ACF.
Read the ACF and PACF to identify candidate orders: the lag 1 and lag 12 spikes point to the SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 model. The automatic search and the simpler ARMA and ARIMA models are included as alternative candidates.
Estimate by maximum likelihood: ARIMA() in fable, under both treatments of the COVID months.
Diagnose the residuals against the white noise standard: Ljung and Box tests, residual plots, ACF and histogram.
Forecast only if the diagnostics pass; otherwise return to step 3.

Finally, a model that survives the loop must still beat the benchmarks on the test set before it earns its place. In this report, models that fail step 5 are still forecast on the test set, but only as reference points showing why the loop matters. They are not candidates for the final model.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
4.2 The COVID problem
ARIMA models assume that one set of parameters describes the whole series. The COVID window breaks this in two ways. First, the April 2020 collapse produces residuals many times larger than normal, which inflates \(\hat\sigma^2\) and therefore every prediction interval. Second, the estimation tries to explain the shock and the recovery with the same MA and AR terms that describe normal month-to-month behaviour, which pulls the coefficients away from their usual values. Simply deleting the COVID months is not possible, because an ARIMA model needs equally spaced observations.
Two designs are compared:

Design A (COVID kept): fit every model to the observed series, including the COVID months.
Design B (COVID as missing): replace March 2020 to March 2022 by NA. The ARIMA likelihood is computed with the Kalman filter, which skips missing observations and simply runs the prediction step through the gap, so the parameters are estimated only from the pre-COVID and post-COVID months while the time ordering is kept intact. The benchmark methods also cope with missing values (for example, seasonal naive uses the last observed value for each month).

This is a deliberately simple treatment of the break. A more structural treatment with intervention variables is left for Project 3.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
9.1 Key findings

Seasonality is the dominant and most stable feature of the series. The seasonal shape barely changed even through the COVID years, which is why the seasonal naive method is hard to beat and why the non-seasonal ARMA and ARIMA models perform poorly.
How the break is handled matters more than which ARIMA model is chosen. With the COVID months kept (Design A), the seasonal ARIMA models were worse than the seasonal naive benchmark on the test set and much worse in cross-validation. The cause is a residual variance inflated by about 134 times, a seasonal MA coefficient pushed to the invertibility boundary (-1.000), and point forecasts pushed upwards by the bias adjustment.
With the COVID window treated as missing (Design B), the Box and Jenkins airline model was the only model to pass the full loop and beat the benchmarks: it passed the diagnostic step and performed best, with a test RMSE of 101.6 thousand nights (MAPE 4.25%), white noise residuals and well calibrated prediction intervals. It also had the lowest cross-validated error at every horizon from 1 to 12 months.
A lower AICc did not guarantee better forecasts. The automatically selected seasonal model had a lower AICc than the hand identified model but higher test RMSE, so the simpler model identified from the ACF and PACF was preferred.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
9.2 Issues and limitations

Choice of COVID window. The window (March 2020 to March 2022) follows the national state of disaster. The data suggest the recovery continued after April 2022, so some post-COVID months still carry the recovery trend into the training data. A sensitivity check with a window ending in December 2022 would test how much this matters.
Treating the shock as missing discards information. Setting 25 months to missing throws away real data, and the approach would not work for a shock at the very end of a series. An intervention model (a level shift or a ramp with a gradual recovery) would use those months instead of ignoring them; this is the starting point for Project 3.
Level shift after COVID. Demand has recovered to slightly below its pre-COVID level. The differenced models adapt to this because they forecast from the most recent level, but the mean benchmark only did reasonably well because the recovered level happens to sit near the long-run average, which would not hold in general.
MASE scaling. The MASE denominator uses an in-sample period that contains the COVID collapse, so the MASE values are deflated. RMSE and MAPE were used as the main measures.
Bias adjustment. Back-transforming with the mean (bias adjusted) forecast is the right choice when the forecasts are added up, for example into annual totals, but it makes the forecasts very sensitive to an inflated \(\hat\sigma^2\). This was a large part of the failure of Design A and is easy to miss.
Short post-COVID history. Only about two years of post-COVID data are in the training set, and the test set is two years long, so the conclusions rest on a fairly short stretch of “normal” data.

title: Week 02
text:
Stationary and Random Walks Generally I found this weeks work quite intuitive. Generally the weeks are moving quite slowly with small amounts of theory covered everything. At first when I revised this weeks content, I found the concept of growing uncertainty confusing because I assumed that as we forecast further into the future, the uncertainty would simply continue increasing in the same way for all time-series models. I initially struggled to understand why the prediction intervals for a random walk continue to widen indefinitely, while those of a stationary AR(1) model eventually level off. I now understand that the difference comes from how each process responds to shocks. In a random walk, shocks accumulate over time, meaning that the further ahead we forecast, the more uncertainty builds up. In a stationary AR(1) process, however, the effects of shocks gradually disappear and the process returns towards its long-run mean. Therefore, although uncertainty initially increases as the forecasting horizon grows, it eventually reaches a finite limit. This helped me understand that forecasting further into the future does not always mean uncertainty grows without bound; it depends on whether the underlying process is stationary or non-stationary.

text:
NoteExecutive summary



Title: Volatility of the South African rand with ARCH and GARCH models
Section and topic: Section 1. Conditional variance models: stylised facts of returns, testing for ARCH effects, ARCH, GARCH and asymmetric GARCH models, volatility forecasting.
Type of project: Implementation (own maximum likelihood code for GARCH(1,1), checked against rugarch and by a small simulation study) and model comparison on real-world data. The Value-at-Risk backtest is an idea not covered in the lectures.
Question: Do daily USD/ZAR exchange rate returns show volatility clustering, and which conditional variance model gives the most reliable one-day-ahead risk forecasts?
Data: Real-world, publicly available data: the South African rand to US dollar spot exchange rate (FRED series DEXSFUS, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System), daily, January 2010 to September 2026. Full source details are in Section 2.1.
Methods: Exploratory analysis of the stylised facts; Ljung and Box and ARCH LM tests; the Box and Jenkins loop applied to the mean and the variance equation; ARCH(1), GARCH(1,1) with normal and Student t errors, and GJR-GARCH(1,1) with Student t errors; my own implementation of the GARCH(1,1) likelihood; a rolling out-of-sample evaluation of 1000 one-day-ahead forecasts, scored by Value-at-Risk backtests (Kupiec and Christoffersen tests), quantile loss and QLIKE, against historical simulation and constant variance benchmarks.
Key findings: The returns show all the stylised facts: almost no autocorrelation in the returns themselves, strong autocorrelation in squared returns, and fat tails. ARCH(1) fails the residual diagnostics, while the GARCH(1,1) models capture the clustering with a very persistent variance. Student t errors fit far better than normal errors. The detailed results of the backtest, including which models give correctly calibrated VaR, are in Section 9.1.
What I would do differently: Use a longer test period so that the 1% VaR tests have more power, and compare GARCH with a regime-switching model of volatility in a potnential future project or comaprison.
Detailed analysis: the sections below.

section: 2.2 Reading the data and computing returns
text:
2.2 Reading the data and computing returns
The code downloads the series the first time the document is rendered and saves it as usdzar_fred.csv. If the download fails (for example without an internet connection), download the CSV manually from the FRED page above and save it in the same folder as this file under that name.


Code
if (!file.exists(data_file)) {
  fred_url <- paste0("https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=DEXSFUS",
                     "&cosd=", start_date, "&coed=", end_date)
  download.file(fred_url, data_file, mode = "wb")
}

fx_raw <- read.csv(data_file, na.strings = c(".", ""))
names(fx_raw) <- c("date", "rate")

fx <- fx_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date), rate = as.numeric(rate)) |>
  filter(!is.na(rate), date >= start_date, date <= end_date) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(r = 100 * (log(rate) - lag(log(rate)))) |>
  filter(!is.na(r)) |>
  mutate(day = row_number())

# tsibble indexed by trading day (the calendar dates are irregular
# because of weekends and US public holidays)
fx_ts <- fx |> as_tsibble(index = day)

r <- fx$r
n <- length(r)


Days on which FRED records no rate (US public holidays) are dropped, so returns are measured from one trading day to the next. The return is defined as
\[
r_t = 100 \times (\log P_t - \log P_{t-1}),
\]
where \(P_t\) is the number of rand per US dollar. A positive return means the rand weakened against the dollar. The analysis uses 4,188 daily returns from 05 January 2010 to 30 September 2026.
I work with log returns rather than plain differences of the rate, \(P_t - P_{t-1}\), for three reasons. First, log returns are scale-free: the rand moved from about R7.31 to R16.42 per dollar over the sample, so a 10-cent move is a 1.4% change at the start but only 0.6% at the end, and plain differences would treat these as the same shock. Second, because the size of rand moves grows with the level of the rate, plain differences show a variance that rises over time because of the trend in the level rather than volatility clustering (Figure 1), which would contaminate the variance equation. Third, multiplied by 100, a log return is approximately the percentage change, and log returns add across days, so a multi-day return is the sum of the daily ones.


Code
p_diff <- ggplot(fx |> mutate(d = rate - lag(rate)), aes(date, d)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Daily change (rand)")

p_logr <- ggplot(fx, aes(date, r)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Daily log return (%)")

p_diff + p_logr








Figure 1: Left: plain daily differences of the rate (rand). Right: daily log returns (%). The plain differences fan out as the rate rises; the log returns do not.

  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 80,

The excess kurtosis of 1.88 and the S-shaped QQ plot in Figure 3 show fat tails: there are many more very small and very large returns than a normal distribution allows. The Jarque and Bera statistic is 651.4 (p < 0.001), so normality is rejected decisively. Part of this is a direct consequence of volatility clustering: a mixture of calm days with a small variance and turbulent days with a large variance has fatter tails than any single normal distribution. Whether returns are still fat-tailed after allowing for a changing variance is a separate question that the Student t models answer below.

text:
3.3 Dependence in returns and in squared returns


Code
p1 <- fx_ts |> ACF(r, lag_max = 50) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Returns")
p2 <- fx_ts |> ACF(r^2, lag_max = 50) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Squared returns")
p3 <- fx_ts |> ACF(abs(r), lag_max = 50) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Absolute returns")
p1 / p2 / p3








Figure 4: ACF of returns, squared returns and absolute returns, up to 50 trading days.





Figure 4 is the key plot of the project. The returns themselves have almost no autocorrelation: the largest absolute autocorrelation in the first 20 lags is only 0.042. The squared and absolute returns, in contrast, have positive autocorrelations that are significant at every lag shown and decay very slowly. This is the signature of volatility clustering: the direction of tomorrow’s move is close to unpredictable, but its size depends strongly on recent sizes. The Ljung and Box test on 20 lags gives Q = 31.6 (p 0.048) for the returns and Q = 417.2 (p < 0.001) for the squared returns.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
section: 5.1 The Box and Jenkins loop for returns
text:
5.1 The Box and Jenkins loop for returns
The project follows the Box and Jenkins workflow from the notes, applied to both equations of the model:

Plot the data: done in the exploratory analysis.
Difference until approximately stationary: working with log returns is the first difference of the log exchange rate. The returns fluctuate around a constant mean, so no further differencing is needed.
Read the ACF and PACF to identify candidate orders: for the mean equation the ACF of the returns is close to zero at all lags, so a constant mean, ARMA(0,0), is used. For the variance equation the slowly decaying ACF of squared returns suggests that a low order ARCH model will not be enough and that GARCH(1,1) is the natural candidate, since it is an ARCH(\(\infty\)) model with geometrically decaying weights.
Estimate by maximum likelihood: with rugarch, and with my own code for GARCH(1,1) (Section 6).
Diagnose residuals against the white noise standard: the standardised residuals \(\hat z_t = \hat\varepsilon_t / \hat\sigma_t\) should show no autocorrelation (mean equation adequate) and their squares should show no autocorrelation (variance equation adequate).
Forecast only if diagnostics pass; otherwise return to step 3.

Finally, a model that survives the loop must still beat the benchmarks out of sample (Section 7).

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
5.2 Candidate models
All models have a constant mean, \(r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t\) with \(\varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t\), and differ in the variance equation and in the distribution of \(z_t\):



Table 2: The four candidate models.










Model
Variance equation
Distribution of \(z_t\)




ARCH(1)
\(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha \varepsilon_{t-1}^2\)
Normal


GARCH(1,1) normal
\(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta \sigma_{t-1}^2\)
Normal


GARCH(1,1) t
as above
Standardised Student t with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom


GJR-GARCH(1,1) t
\(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + (\alpha + \gamma I_{t-1}) \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta \sigma_{t-1}^2\), with \(I_{t-1} = 1\) if \(\varepsilon_{t-1} < 0\)

The GJR model allows good and bad news to affect volatility differently. For a share price the usual finding is that falls (negative returns) raise volatility more than rises. sim_garch11 <- function(n, mu, omega, alpha, beta, burn = 500) {
  N <- n + burn
  z <- rnorm(N); e <- s2 <- numeric(N)
  s2[1] <- omega / (1 - alpha - beta)
  e[1]  <- sqrt(s2[1]) * z[1]

    e[t]  <- sqrt(s2[t]) * z[t]

  mu + e[(burn + 1):N]

7.1 Design
In-sample fit does not answer the research question, which is about forecasts. The last 1000 trading days (from 30 September 2022 to 30 September 2026) are used as a test period. For each day in the test period, every model produces a one-day-ahead forecast of the mean and standard deviation using only data up to the previous day. The GARCH models are re-estimated every 25 trading days on an expanding window, which keeps the evaluation free of temporal leakage.
From each forecast distribution I compute the VaR at four levels: the 1% and 5% quantiles (losses for someone holding dollars when the rand strengthens) and the 95% and 99% quantiles (losses for someone who needs dollars, such as an importer, when the rand weakens). For Student t models,
\[
\text{VaR}_{p,t} = \hat\mu_{t|t-1} + \hat\sigma_{t|t-1} \, t_{\nu}^{-1}(p) \sqrt{(\nu - 2)/\nu},
\]
where the last factor rescales the t distribution to unit variance.
Two benchmarks without a GARCH variance are included, in the spirit of the benchmark methods in the notes:

Historical simulation (HS): the VaR is the empirical quantile of the previous 250 returns.
Rolling normal: a normal distribution with the mean and variance of the previous 250 returns.

The ARCH(1) model failed the residual diagnostics, so following step 6 it is not part of the forecast comparison.

7.2 Backtest tests
For each model and level, a hit is a day on which the realised return falls beyond the VaR (below it for the 1% and 5% levels, above it for the 95% and 99% levels). Under a correct model the hits are independent Bernoulli(\(p^*\)) variables, where \(p^* = p\) for the lower tail and \(p^* = 1 - p\) for the upper tail. I implemented two standard likelihood ratio tests.

Kupiec unconditional coverage test: is the hit rate equal to \(p^*\)? With \(x\) hits in \(T\) days and \(\hat\pi = x / T\), \(LR_{uc} = -2 \left[ (T - x)\log(1 - p^*) + x \log p^* - (T - x)\log(1 - \hat\pi) - x \log \hat\pi \right] \sim \chi^2_1 .\)
Christoffersen conditional coverage test: adds a test of independence, comparing a first-order Markov chain for the hits with an independent sequence, so that clustered hits are detected. \(LR_{cc} = LR_{uc} + LR_{ind} \sim \chi^2_2\).



Code
kupiec_test <- function(hits, p) {
  n <- length(hits); x <- sum(hits); phat <- x / n
  ll0 <- (n - x) * log(1 - p) + x * log(p)
  ll1 <- if (x == 0 || x == n) 0 else (n - x) * log(1 - phat) + x * log(phat)
  lr  <- -2 * (ll0 - ll1)
  c(hits = x, expected = n * p, LR_uc = lr, p_uc = pchisq(lr, 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
}

christoffersen_test <- function(hits, p) {
  h0 <- hits[-length(hits)]; h1 <- hits[-1]
  n00 <- sum(h0 == 0 & h1 == 0); n01 <- sum(h0 == 0 & h1 == 1)
  n10 <- sum(h0 == 1 & h1 == 0); n11 <- sum(h0 == 1 & h1 == 1)
  pi01 <- n01 / (n00 + n01)
  pi11 <- if ((n10 + n11) > 0) n11 / (n10 + n11) else 0
  pi1  <- (n01 + n11) / (n00 + n01 + n10 + n11)
  xlogy <- function(x, y) ifelse(x == 0, 0, x * log(y))
  ll_ind <- xlogy(n00, 1 - pi01) + xlogy(n01, pi01) +
            xlogy(n10, 1 - pi11) + xlogy(n11, pi11)
  ll_dep <- xlogy(n00 + n10, 1 - pi1) + xlogy(n01 + n11, pi1)
  lr_ind <- -2 * (ll_dep - ll_ind)
  lr_cc  <- kupiec_test(hits, p)[["LR_uc"]] + lr_ind
  c(p_ind = pchisq(lr_ind, 1, lower.tail = FALSE),
    p_cc  = pchisq(lr_cc, 2, lower.tail = FALSE))
}

At the 1% level, where a correct model should be exceeded about 10 times, the GARCH(1,1) normal model is exceeded 7 times in the lower tail and 10 times in the upper tail, against 4 and 9 for the GARCH(1,1) t model. The normal model is exceeded more often in the extreme tails, which is the practical consequence of the fat tails found in its residuals.
Clustering of exceedances. The benchmarks react slowly to a change in volatility: a window of 250 days gives the same weight to a return from a year ago as to yesterday’s. When volatility jumps, their VaR is too narrow for weeks and the hits bunch together, which is what the Christoffersen test detects; when volatility falls, their VaR stays too wide for a long time (Figure 7). The GARCH VaR bands widen and narrow within days.
Ranking. Averaged over the four levels, the lowest quantile loss is achieved by the GJR-GARCH(1,1) t model, and the lowest QLIKE by the GJR-GARCH(1,1) t model.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
9.1 Key findings

The rand shows all the stylised facts of financial returns: almost no autocorrelation in returns, strong and slowly decaying autocorrelation in squared returns, and fat tails (excess kurtosis 1.9). The ARCH LM test confirms a time-varying variance (p < 0.001).
The Box and Jenkins loop rejected ARCH(1) because ARCH structure remained in its standardised residuals, and led to GARCH(1,1).
Volatility is highly persistent: \(\hat\alpha + \hat\beta\) = 0.9874, a half-life of about 55 trading days.
Student t errors are clearly better than normal errors (\(\hat\nu\) = 11.0), so even after removing volatility clustering, extreme days are more common than a normal distribution implies.
Asymmetry: \(\hat\gamma\) = -0.051 (p < 0.001). There is significant asymmetry in how depreciation and appreciation shocks affect volatility.
Out of sample, the preferred model by quantile loss is GJR-GARCH(1,1) t and by QLIKE GJR-GARCH(1,1) t. The number of rejected VaR tests (out of four levels) was 3 for GARCH(1,1) t against 0 for historical simulation and 2 for the rolling normal benchmark.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
9.2 Issues and limitations

Power of the tests. With 1000 test days, a correct 1% VaR is expected to be exceeded only 10 times, so the Kupiec test has little power to separate a 1% model from, say, a 1.5% model. A model that “passes” is not proven correct.
Tests with a large sample. The residual tests in-sample use more than 4000 observations, so even very small departures from white noise can be significant. I combined the formal tests with the plots and the out-of-sample results rather than relying on p-values alone.
Very high persistence. A persistence close to 1 can be a sign of structural breaks in the level of volatility (for example a calmer period after 2020) rather than true long memory, as discussed in the notes. A model with a regime change in volatility would be a natural alternative, and this is the subject of Project 4.
Data choices. FRED noon rates in New York miss moves that happen during South African trading hours after the New York fix, and dropping US holidays makes some returns cover two days. Neither should affect the conclusions much, but a Johannesburg close series would be a useful check.
Refitting every 25 days rather than daily saves time but means the parameters lag slightly behind; the volatility itself is still updated every day.
VaR is only one risk measure. It says nothing about how large losses are once the VaR is exceeded. Expected shortfall would be the natural extension.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
9.3 What I would do differently
I would use a longer test period, add expected shortfall to the backtest, and compare GARCH with a hidden Markov model that lets volatility switch between a small number of regimes (Project 4), using the same returns and the same backtest so that the two approaches can be compared directly.

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 1: The forecasting process (15)
Context: producing sales forecasts for several products of a large biscuit manufacturer.
1. Problem definition. The aim is to forecast future sales for the company’s range of biscuits so that it can make strategic and operational decisions about how, when and where to sell and produce. This means pinning down exactly what is forecast: which products (individual biscuit lines or product families), at what level (national, regional or by retailer), in what units, how far ahead and how often (e.g. weekly forecasts for production scheduling, monthly forecasts a year ahead for ingredient purchasing and budgeting). This is done by talking to the people who will use the forecasts (production, procurement, sales and marketing, finance).
2. Data collection. For each product, collect a record of how many units were sold each period (e.g. monthly), building up a historical time series that can be used to forecast future sales. Also collect information on factors that help explain sales: prices, promotions, advertising campaigns, product launches and competitor activity, along with calendar effects such as public holidays, school holidays and weekends. Knowledge from the sales team about one-off events (stock-outs, factory shutdowns, a large once-off order) is also recorded so the data can be interpreted correctly.
3. Data analysis. This is the exploratory stage, done before any model is fitted. Plot each series and look for trend, seasonality (e.g. peaks before Christmas and Easter), cycles, outliers and structural breaks; check whether a transformation (e.g. logs) or differencing is needed; examine the ACF/PACF; and look at how sales relate to drivers such as promotions, in order to understand consumer demand at different times of the year. The arrow back from model selection shows the process is iterative: what is learnt when fitting a model can send us back to look at the data again.
4. Model selection and fitting. Based on the patterns found in the data analysis (and the ACF and PACF, which show the autocorrelation structure), choose candidate models, e.g. exponential smoothing (such as Holt–Winters for trending, seasonal products), ARIMA/seasonal ARIMA, state space models, or regression models with promotion and price effects, and estimate their parameters on the historical data.
5. Model validation. Assess how accurate each model’s forecasts are. Split the data so that a hold-out (test) set is kept back, and compare forecasts with the actual values using metrics such as RMSE, MAE and MAPE, using validation approaches such as rolling-origin (time series cross-validation) or sliding windows. Residuals should also be checked to make sure they look like white noise. The best-performing model is chosen.
6. Forecasting model deployment. Put the forecasts into practical use, since the whole point of forecasting is to support decisions. The chosen model is built into the company’s planning systems and produces forecasts (with prediction intervals) on a regular schedule, which are used for decisions such as production planning, which products to invest in or refine, and advertising strategies targeted at the products and times of year where sales are strongest.
7. Monitoring forecasting model performance. Continuously compare forecasts with actual sales as they come in and track the forecast errors over time, to detect bias or deterioration, for instance when consumer preferences change or a competitor changes strategy. This monitoring could be automated (e.g. an automated system or AI agent that is fed new data, updates the forecasts and flags when errors drift or market changes occur). When performance deteriorates, the model is re-estimated or the process returns to an earlier stage.

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 2: Expected time patterns (8)
(a) Monthly sales of computer hard drives at a local store (10 years). Over the 10 years I would expect a trend: sales would initially increase steadily as computers became more common and people bought hard drives to keep their computers going for longer, but then trend downwards as technology develops and newer products (e.g. solid-state drives and cloud storage) replace them. There would also be seasonality within each year, e.g. at the beginning of the year when school and university go back, and around Black Friday and the festive season. (Because the data are monthly, within-month effects such as payday are not visible.)
(b) Hourly pulse rate of a person for one week. A strong daily (24-hour) seasonal pattern: pulse rate is elevated during the day while the person is moving around and active, and drops to a resting level while they sleep at night. If the person exercises every day, there will also be a regular daily spike in heart rate at that time. Little or no trend would be expected over a single week.
(c) Daily sales at a fast-food store for six months. A weekly seasonal pattern, with increased demand and sales over weekends (Friday nights to Sunday), plus increases around public holidays (and possibly month-end/payday). Six months is quite a short period, so long-term trends would be hard to see.
(d) Weekly electricity consumption for your local area (10 years). A strong annual seasonal pattern: in South Africa consumption is highest in winter (heating, longer nights) with a possible smaller summer peak from air-conditioning, and dips over the December holidays when businesses and industry shut down. There would also be a trend reflecting population growth and development, possibly offset in recent years by load-shedding, higher tariffs and rooftop solar.

Question 3: Matching series to ACFs (12)
The key idea is: a trend makes neighbouring values (even ones far apart) similar, so the ACF starts very high and decays slowly while staying positive; seasonality/cycles make the ACF oscillate, with peaks at lags equal to the period; and a series with neither has small autocorrelations that die out quickly.

Matching each series to its ACF

No seasonality or strong trend, just a slight downward drift and irregular variation. The ACF has small-to-moderate positive values that die out without any regular oscillation, consistent with a weakly persistent, non-seasonal series.


2. Accidental deaths in USA (monthly)

Clear monthly seasonality with period 12 and no trend. ACF A has a large positive spike at lag 12 and strong negative values around lag 6 (half a seasonal cycle), the pattern of a period-12 seasonal series.

Strong upward trend plus seasonality. The trend produces very large positive autocorrelations that decay slowly (ACF D starts near 0.9 and stays high); the seasonality shows as a small bump around lag 12.

Figure 3: Seasonal plot: each line is one year.









Trend: sales increase strongly over time, consistent with the shop expanding its premises, products and staff. The growth accelerates in 1992–1993.
Seasonality: a very strong annual pattern. Sales build up through November and peak sharply every December (Christmas tourists), then drop back in January. A smaller secondary peak occurs each March from 1988 onward (the surf festival). There is no March peak in 1987 because the festival only started in 1988.
Changing variance: the size of the seasonal fluctuations grows with the level of the series (the December peaks become enormous), so the seasonality is multiplicative rather than additive.
Unusual features: sales in 1990–1991 stalled: December 1990 (30114) was below December 1989 (34061), and January and March 1991 were lower than a year earlier, breaking the upward trend (possibly an economic downturn or poor tourist season). There are also some months that deviate from the usual seasonal shape, e.g. the unusually high March 1990 and the very sharp jump in December 1992 and 1993.



(b) Why take logarithms? (2)
The variance of the series increases with its level: the seasonal swings are proportional to the level (multiplicative seasonality). Most models (and linear regression) assume constant variance and additive components. Taking logarithms stabilises the variance and turns multiplicative effects into additive ones (\(\log(T \times S \times E) = \log T + \log S + \log E\)), and turns exponential growth into a linear trend (Figure 4).

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 6: IBM daily closing prices (4)

Time plot: the series does not fluctuate around a constant mean. It wanders up from about 450 to 600, then falls sharply to about 300–400, with long local “trends”. There is no level to which it reverts, which is typical of a random walk.
ACF: the autocorrelations start close to 1 and decay extremely slowly (still about 0.8 at lag 25). For a stationary series the ACF should drop to zero quickly; a slowly decaying ACF is the classic sign of non-stationarity.
PACF: there is a single very large spike at lag 1 of almost exactly 1, with all other partial autocorrelations negligible. This indicates \(Y_t \approx Y_{t-1} + e_t\), i.e. an AR(1) with \(\phi_1 \approx 1\), i.e. a unit root.

Together these show the series is non-stationary and should be differenced (first differences \(Y_t - Y_{t-1}\), i.e. the daily price changes, are likely to be stationary).

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 7: Strikes in the USA, 1951–1980 (16)


Show code
strikes_raw <- read_excel(data_file, sheet = 3, .name_repair = "minimal")
strikes <- ts(c(strikes_raw[[2]], strikes_raw[[5]]), start = 1951)



(a) Why ARIMA(0,1,1)? (3)

Original seriesFirst differences




Show code
ggtsdisplay(strikes, main = "Number of strikes", xlab = "Year")








Figure 6: Strikes series: time plot, ACF and PACF.









Show code
ggtsdisplay(diff(strikes), main = "Differenced number of strikes", xlab = "Year")








Figure 7: First differences of the strikes series: time plot, ACF and PACF.









The original series (Figure 6) wanders: it falls from about 5 000 in the early 1950s to about 3 400 in the early 1960s, then rises to around 6 000 in the 1970s, without reverting to a fixed mean. The ACF decays slowly (0.73 at lag 1 and still positive for several lags), and the PACF has one large spike at lag 1. The series is non-stationary, so it should be differenced once (\(d = 1\)).
The differenced series (Figure 7) fluctuates around a constant mean of about zero with roughly constant variance, so it appears stationary. Its ACF has a single negative spike at lag 1 (-0.34, close to the \(\pm 2/\sqrt{n} \approx \pm 0.37\) bound) and is negligible thereafter (the ACF “cuts off” after lag 1), while the PACF decays. This is the signature of an MA(1) process for the differences (\(q = 1\), \(p = 0\)).

Hence ARIMA(0,1,1) is appropriate. (No constant is included since the differences have mean approximately zero, so there is no persistent trend in the series.)


(b) Backshift operator form (2)
With \(B Y_t = Y_{t-1}\), the ARIMA(0,1,1) model is \[(1 - B)\,Y_t = (1 + \theta_1 B)\, e_t \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Y_t = Y_{t-1} + e_t + \theta_1 e_{t-1},\] where \(e_t\) is white noise.






Tip



R uses the “\(+\theta\)” sign convention; some textbooks write \((1 - \theta_1 B)e_t\), in which case the sign of the estimate is reversed.

Question 8: Bituminous coal production (10)

(a) What sort of ARIMA model? (3)
The model \(Y_t = c + \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{t-2} + \phi_3 Y_{t-3} + \phi_4 Y_{t-4} + e_t\) is an autoregressive model of order 4 on the undifferenced series with no moving-average terms: an ARIMA(4,0,0), i.e. AR(4), with \(p = 4\), \(d = 0\), \(q = 0\).


(b) Why was this model chosen? (1)
The time plot fluctuates around a fairly constant mean (roughly 300–630 million tons, no persistent trend) and the ACF dies down quickly, so the series appears stationary and no differencing is needed (\(d=0\)). The ACF decays in a damped, sine-wave-like fashion (typical of an AR process), while the PACF has significant spikes at lags 1 and 4 and cuts off after lag 4, which identifies an AR(4) model.


(c) Forecasts for 1969–1971 (6)

title: ARCH and GARCH Lab
text:
Overview of the key concepts
Financial and interest-rate series share a few stylised facts: the series itself (or its changes) shows little autocorrelation, but its squares or absolute values are strongly autocorrelated. This is volatility clustering: large moves follow large moves and calm follows calm. Returns are also heavier-tailed than a normal distribution.
An ARMA model only describes the conditional mean, and assumes a constant variance. ARCH and GARCH models add an equation for the conditional variance:
\[
\varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} (0,1)
\]

ARCH(1): \(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2\). Today’s variance depends on yesterday’s squared shock.
GARCH(1,1): \(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2\). Adding the lagged variance gives long memory in volatility with only one extra parameter. Persistence is measured by \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1\); the variance is covariance-stationary only if this is below 1.

In practice the two are combined: an ARMA model for the mean with GARCH errors, estimated jointly by maximum likelihood. The conditional distribution of \(z_t\) can be normal or a standardised \(t\) to allow fat tails.
Diagnostics work on two kinds of residuals. The raw residuals \(\hat\varepsilon_t\) still contain the changing variance, so the ACF of \(\hat\varepsilon_t^2\) shows whether ARCH effects are present. The standardised residuals \(\hat z_t = \hat\varepsilon_t / \hat\sigma_t\) should be white noise with no remaining structure in their squares if the model is adequate. Ljung-Box tests on \(\hat z_t\) and \(\hat z_t^2\) formalise this.
A fitted GARCH model gives a conditional forecast distribution for the next observation, which lets us compute probabilities of extreme moves given yesterday’s information. This is the basis of Value-at-Risk.

(a) Model. arma(1,0) + garch(1,0) is an AR(1) mean with ARCH(1) errors. In the notation of the R output, with \(Y_t\) = Del.Tbill:
\[

\varepsilon_t &= \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0,1), \\

(a) acf(res) plots the sample autocorrelations of the raw residuals \(\hat\varepsilon_t = Y_t - \hat\mu - \widehat{\text{ar1}}\, Y_{t-1}\). It checks the mean equation. Almost all lags lie within the bounds; lag 2 is borderline (-0.14) and the Ljung-Box p-value is 0.075. The AR(1) mean is adequate, though only just at the 10% level.
(b) acf(res^2) plots the autocorrelations of the squared raw residuals. These are still strongly autocorrelated (lag 4 is 0.55; Ljung-Box p < 0.001). This is not a sign of poor fit. The raw residuals are \(\sigma_t z_t\), so they still carry the time-varying variance by construction. The plot tells us that GARCH effects are present in the series, which is the reason for modelling the variance.
(c) acf(res_std^2) plots the autocorrelations of the squared standardised residuals \(\hat z_t^2 = (\hat\varepsilon_t / \hat\sigma_t)^2\). If the variance equation has captured the clustering, these should be white noise. They nearly are: the largest spike is lag 4 (0.16) and the Ljung-Box p-value is 0.273. ARCH(1) removes most of the volatility clustering. The lag-4 spike in quarterly data hints at more persistence than one lag of ARCH can capture.
(d) garch.model.Tbill@sigma.t holds the fitted conditional standard deviations \(\hat\sigma_t = \sqrt{\hat\omega + \hat\alpha_1 \hat\varepsilon_{t-1}^2}\), one per quarter. They range from 0.58 to 3.86. Dividing the residuals by them gives the standardised residuals.
(e) plot(res_std). Compared with the raw residuals, the bursts of large values around 1980 have been flattened, so standardising has done its job. Two things stand out:

A few large standardised residuals remain (1986 Q1 (3.09), 1994 Q2 (3.44)). They happen in calm periods, where ARCH(1) predicted a small \(\sigma_t\) because the previous shock was small. A moderate move then looks extreme. ARCH(1) forgets too quickly.
The tails are heavier than normal (kurtosis 4.62, Shapiro-Wilk p < 0.001). A \(t\) conditional distribution would be more realistic.

That is the level effect from Problem 1 showing through: as rates rose, the variance kept rising, and a GARCH model can only express this as non-stationary volatility.

Advantages of log differences.

They remove the level effect. A log difference is approximately a percentage change. A 1-point move means much more at a 2% rate than at 15%. On the log scale changes are comparable across decades, so volatility depends mainly on past shocks, which is exactly what GARCH assumes.
Stationary variance. The GARCH persistence drops below 1, so the model has a finite unconditional variance and forecasts revert to a long-run level.
Positivity. Forecasts transformed back with exp() can never give a negative interest rate.

The AIC values for the two responses cannot be compared, because they are on different scales. The comparison has to rest on the diagnostics and the stability of the fitted variance.

Two observations. First, the GARCH model had already raised the forecast volatility to 1.7 times the two-year sample standard deviation, because the preceding week (including a -5.4% fall on the Friday) was turbulent. Second, the heavy tails matter enormously: under a normal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation the probability would be 5.3e-40, i.e. effectively impossible.

title: ARCH and GARCH Lab
text:
Implementation in R
To understand what garchFit is doing, I wrote the AR(1)/ARCH(1) Gaussian log-likelihood myself and maximised it with optim, using the Del.Tbill data from Part A.
For \(t = 2, \dots, n\), with \(\varepsilon_t = (Y_t - m) - \phi (Y_{t-1} - m)\) and \(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2\):
\[
\ell(m, \phi, \omega, \alpha_1) = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_t \left[\log(2\pi) + \log\sigma_t^2 + \frac{\varepsilon_t^2}{\sigma_t^2}\right].
\]
I parametrise with the mean \(m\) (not the intercept), and optimise over \(\log\omega\) and \(\text{logit}(\alpha_1)\), so that \(\omega > 0\) and \(0 < \alpha_1 < 1\) hold automatically. The recursion starts with \(\sigma_1^2\) equal to the sample variance.


Code
arch1_nll <- function(theta, y) {
  m <- theta[1]; phi <- theta[2]
  omega <- exp(theta[3]); alpha <- plogis(theta[4])
  n <- length(y)
  e <- numeric(n)
  e[1] <- y[1] - m
  e[-1] <- (y[-1] - m) - phi * (y[-n] - m)
  s2 <- numeric(n); s2[1] <- var(y)
  for (t in 2:n) s2[t] <- omega + alpha * e[t - 1]^2
  -sum(dnorm(e, 0, sqrt(s2), log = TRUE))
}

y <- as.numeric(Del.Tbill)
own <- optim(c(mean(y), 0.2, log(var(y) / 2), 0), arch1_nll, y = y, method = "BFGS")
own_est <- c(mean = own$par[1], ar1 = own$par[2],
             omega = exp(own$par[3]), alpha1 = plogis(own$par[4]))

fg <- coef(garch.model.Tbill)
compare <- rbind(
  "Own MLE" = c(own_est, `-logL` = own$value),
  "fGarch"  = c(mean = unname(fg["mu"] / (1 - fg["ar1"])), fg[c("ar1", "omega", "alpha1")],
                `-logL` = garch.model.Tbill@fit$llh))

title: ARCH and GARCH Lab
text:
Reflection
What was most challenging: Reading the fGarch output correctly. Three things caught me out: mu is the intercept rather than the mean, the AIC from summary() is divided by the sample size (so it cannot be compared with arima() until multiplied by \(n\)), and "std" is a \(t\) rescaled to unit variance, so the probability in Part B needs the \(\sqrt{(\nu-2)/\nu}\) correction if computed with pt(). Understanding the different jobs of raw and standardised residuals also took time: significant autocorrelation in res^2 is expected, while the same in res_std^2 would mean the model has failed.
What I now understand: A GARCH model is a model for the conditional variance, and its value shows up in conditional statements, such as the probability of a crash given yesterday’s information. Transformations matter as much as model choice. On the raw T-bill changes, a GARCH(1,1) produced an explosive variance because volatility was tied to the level of rates; on log changes the same model gave stationary, sensible persistence. Choosing the right scale for the data fixed a problem that no extra GARCH term could. I also saw that the conditional distribution is not a detail: with the same mean and volatility forecast, the \(t\) and normal assumptions gave Black Monday probabilities about 35 orders of magnitude apart.
Advantages and limitations of the methods:

Advantages: GARCH models capture volatility clustering with few parameters, give one-step-ahead volatility forecasts and conditional probabilities directly, and combine naturally with an ARMA mean. With \(t\) errors they also allow for fat tails.
Limitations: Variance responds only to the size of past shocks, not to their sign or to the level of the series (the level effect in T-bill rates needed a transformation instead). The model is symmetric, so it cannot capture the leverage effect where falls raise volatility more than rises (GJR-GARCH or EGARCH would). Good in-sample diagnostics say nothing about events outside the sample’s experience: the Black Monday model passed every check yet still put the crash at roughly a once-in-two-centuries event. Model choice between ARCH and GARCH can also be ambiguous when AIC and BIC disagree, as in Part B (c).
